title: Psychedelic psychological first aid

source.dataset: psychonautwiki_db.zip (psychonautwiki.db, SQLite export provided by Hany, file dated 2026-11-25)

plain_text:
Psychedelic psychological first aid is defined as any behavioral technique which provides an acute and immediate assistance for behavior in psychedelic cognition. These techniques encompass both dissuading dysfunctional behavior and encouraging functional behavior.

This page lists and describes the various psychedelic psychological first aid techniques.

Dealing with difficult experiences:

In many cases temporary difficult experiences encountered during a psychedelic journey can be resolved with relatively simple techniques. 

Some general suggestions for changing the mood of a psychedelic trip are given below:

*Change the music
*Change physical location - sit in a different seat, go to a different room, move inside/outside
*Change the lighting - turn some lights on/off, change the color of the light if possible, light some candles
*Turn on some funny videos or suitable cartoons
*Watch some relaxing nature videos/documentaries
*Drink some water
*Do some light stretching/yoga
*Do a little dance
*Sing a song
*Do some mindfulness/meditation/breathing exercises
*Play with your pets

Notes for tripsitters:

The nature of a person having a difficult experience is, many times, one of letting go on all levels of a person’s being. It is positive to create a space where it is possible to be open, a space that’s quiet, warm, safe, and beautiful. This space is as important as the sitting/facilitating itself. If possible, have flowers, candles, art and writing supplies, blankets, quiet music and soft light.

If the person wants to speak, if sounds come out uncontrolled, support the expression. This might be: a different or dead language, prayers from the different spiritual traditions, far-out stories and memories, jibberish, animal sounds, looping sentences (repeating over and over the same words), lamenting, cries, or screams.

Respond when needed, do not take over, try to (if appropriate) engage in a calm conversation, responding to fear and anxiety.

Pay attention to the body language while you listen to what’s being expressed verbally and emotionally. Follow the expression of the person. If they have a lot of energy, let the energy move, let it express itself in whatever form: uncontrolled shaking, yoga postures, dancing, ritualistic type of movements, hyperventilation, kundalini type release.

The most appropriate response to a powerful psychedelic crisis might be to just sit quietly with the person, making them feel safe.

If the person is stuck there are several different ways to respond:

*Wait and calm them down through talk, knowing the duration of the substance taken
*Walk with them, talking or not, until they calm down
*Have them express the experience through sound
*Have them move through it, through a physical expression, holding a certain posture or letting the body go
*One could do some deep, focused bodywork, just hold someone (meeting their needs) or gently massage them. Always ask for permission regarding any kind of physical contact.
*The person could recline, eyes closed or blindfolded, being in a safe place, listening to comforting music and grounding the experience.
*If their emotions are overwhelming them, encourage their expression.
*When the person is calm enough or has come back from their difficult psychedelic experience, have art supplies and writing material available.

Reassure them:

#This will pass, this is a process.
#This is an experience other people have had.

Mindfulness

Overview:

Suggestions on how to generate mindfulness as a tripsitter:

*Ask an individual to focus on their breath. Ask them to breath in through the nose and out through the mouth. Ask them to notice the flow of air from the tip of their nostrils all the way down into their lungs and then all the way back out to the lips.   It may be useful to have the individual place one hand on their sternum (where the rib cage meets over the heart) and the other hand on their stomach. This further allows the individual to experience the breath as the rising and falling of their hands provides an additional 'input signal' for the mindfulness exercise.
*Direct an individual to focus on their body. They should try to label how each body part is feeling without attaching a positive or negative significance to the actual feeling. They can perform a 'body scan' where they move their attention through their entire body focusing on the sensations that arise. They can start with their feet, move upwards through the legs, past their chest, down their arms and then up through the neck and the head. A well known technique used in therapy is to have an individual sit in a chair with their feet on the ground. They should focus on how the body is positioned, how the chair feels against their body and how the stability of the ground presses up into the bottom of their feet.
*Direct an individual to focus on their senses. They can describe (out-loud or in their head) what they are seeing, hearing, smelling, touching or tasting. You can direct them to do a 'stream of consciousness' exercise where they speak each thing their attention focuses on.  For example "I see the wood on the table. I hear the birds chirping outside. I see the sofa. I hear the fan running. I feel the floor on my feet. I hear the guitar from the song.  I feel the breeze from the window" etc.

Useful resources

*MAPS Manual: How to Work with Difficult Psychedelic Experiences  Gives information on the following topics:
*#Role of the Sitter or Facilitator
*#Varieties of Psychedelic-Induced Crises
*#Working and Being with Psychedelic Emergencies
*#Aftercare
